MADISON (WKOW) – At Tuesday’s Common Council meeting, Madison alders heard a presentation on the state of homelessness in the city and Dane County. The information carried weight for the local leaders as they decide where to make cuts in the city’s operating budget. Dane County's homeless population rose 18 percent over last year, to 737 people during the last point-in-time count conducted by the Homeless Services Consortium of Dane County . Alders learned that operating expenses and demand for homeless services are higher than before the pandemic. Porchlight's men's emergency shelter on Zier Road has seen its budget balloon from $584,000 in 2019, to nearly $2.9 million this year. Much of that funding increase is supported by the city, though it has used pandemic-era assistance money to support the shelter. Congress has not renewed the money, which will expire next year. The City of Madison is unlikely to be able to offer its own support as it is facing a budget shortfall of around $22 million. The Common Council may call for a referendum to help balance its budget this November. In the interim, the city’s various departments have been instructed to plan for a five percent budget cut. The cut would equate to approximately $800,000 for the city’s Community Development Division which oversees homelessness services. Alders asked several probing questions of Community Development Division Director James O’Keefe who gave the presentation. “I often wonder, why can't all of the churches come together?” Alder Isadore Knox asked. “There shouldn't be a single night [in] any part of town where several church groups could be opening their doors.” Churches provide many homeless services in Madison, and prior to the pandemic the city and Dane County relied on churches as the means to distribute the majority of homelessness resources. Porchlight's men's emergency shelter began in the basement of Grace Episcopal Church on the Capitol Square. It eventually outgrew the location. The church’s reverend doctor Jonathan grieser told 27 News the church cannot be expected to again take on that responsibility. “I would be cautious to assume churches can offer more than they already are,” the reverend said. He noted declines in church attendance and membership over the last few years.
